citations.quote:
A matrix $A\in M_n(F)$ is **invertible** when there is a matrix $B\in M_n(F)$
such that

$$AB=I_n=BA.$$

Such a $B$ is unique and is denoted $A^{-1}$. The **general linear set** is

$$\operatorname{GL}_n(F):=\{A\in M_n(F):A\text{ is invertible}\}.$$

It is the set of units of the ring $M_n(F)$. The fact that it is a group under
matrix multiplication is [[cor-general-linear-group-is-a-group]]. For $n=0$,
the unique empty matrix is $I_0$ and is its own inverse.

Let $\gamma:[a,b]\to\mathbb C$ be a **closed** complex contour, that is a
rectifiable path with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)$
([[def-complex-contours-reversal-concatenation-and-closedness]]), with trace
$\gamma^\ast$, and let $p\in\mathbb C$ with $p\notin\gamma^\ast$. The **winding
number**, or **index**, of $\gamma$ about $p$ is

$$n(\gamma,p):=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_\gamma\frac{dz}{z-p},$$

the complex line integral of
[[def-complex-line-integral-over-a-rectifiable-path]].

The integral exists: $z\mapsto1/(z-p)$ is complex differentiable, hence
continuous, on $\mathbb C\setminus\{p\}$ by
[[thm-algebra-of-complex-derivatives]] and
[[cor-complex-differentiability-implies-continuity]], the trace $\gamma^\ast$ is
contained in that set, and $\gamma$ is rectifiable, so
[[thm-existence-of-complex-line-integrals-on-rectifiable-paths]] applies.

derivations.claim: **Scalar winding and the necessary obstruction.** For a smooth nonzero complex loop $z$, choose one real argument $\psi(0)$ of $z(0)/|z(0)|$ and set $\psi(s)=\psi(0)+\operatorname{Im}\int_0^s z'(a)/z(a)\,da$. Differentiating shows $z(s)/|z(s)|=e^{i\psi(s)}$: both sides have logarithmic derivative $i\operatorname{Im}(z'/z)$ and the same initial value. Also $\operatorname{Re}(z'/z)=(\log|z|)'$, so its real integral over a loop is zero. Closedness gives $\psi(1)-\psi(0)=2\pi k$ for one integer $k$, and the displayed winding is exactly $k$. For a smooth family of nonzero loops, the integral is a continuous integer-valued function, hence constant. If an invertible matrix map fills the disk, take its determinant on concentric circles. Their windings are constant for positive radius and tend to zero as radius tends to zero, since the map is smooth and its determinant stays nonzero near the center. Thus the boundary winding must vanish. This also proves additivity of winding under products of nonzero scalar loops by the product logarithmic derivative.

**Reduce to a special unitary loop.** Apply the finite Gram–Schmidt formulas to the columns of $G$, obtaining a smooth factorization $G=QR$ with $Q\in U(m)$ and $R$ upper triangular with positive real diagonal. Every denominator is the nonzero norm of the next orthogonalized column; independence of the original columns ensures it is positive. The matrices $R_r=(1-r)R+rI$ are invertible upper triangular with positive diagonal, so $Q R_r$ is a smooth homotopy from $G$ to $Q$. Their determinants have the same winding since $\det R_r$ is positive real. If $w(G)=0$, step 1.1 gives a periodic smooth real lift $\psi(s)$ with $\det Q(s)=e^{i\psi(s)}$. The loops $Q(s)\operatorname{diag}(e^{-ir\psi(s)},1,\ldots,1)$ give a smooth homotopy from $Q$ to a loop in $SU(m)$. For $m=1$ this final loop is the constant identity.

**Contract a loop of unit first columns.** Suppose $m\ge2$ and $A(s)$ is a smooth loop in $SU(m)$, with first column $v(s)\in S^{2m-1}$. Choose a point $q$ of that sphere outside both $v(S^1)$ and the point $e_1$. Such a point exists without a selection principle: a smooth loop has a bounded speed $L$ and is covered by $N$ balls of radius $L/N$; in a fixed bounded sphere coordinate cube, whose dimension $d=2m-1>1$, their coordinate box volumes have sum at most $C N(L/N)^d$, tending to zero. Finite subadditivity of box volume shows these boxes cannot cover that cube for large $N$. Removing the one additional point $e_1$ does not change this argument. Stereographic projection from $q$ identifies its complement with $\mathbb R^{2m-1}$. Straight-line contraction there from the loop to the image of $e_1$, followed by inverse stereographic projection, gives a smooth map $v(s,r)$ of unit vectors with $v(s,0)=v(s)$ and $v(s,1)=e_1$.

**Lift that contraction with a trace-free matrix ODE.** Write $a=v^*v_r$, which is purely imaginary because $v^*v=1$, and define $K=v_rv^*-v v_r^*-a vv^*-\frac{a}{m-1}(I-vv^*).$ Direct multiplication gives $K^*=-K$, $\operatorname{tr}K=0$, and $Kv=v_r$. For each $s$ solve $F_r=K F$, $F(s,0)=A(s)$, using the series $F=(I+\int_0^r K(r_1)dr_1+\int_{0<r_2<r_1<r}K(r_1)K(r_2)dr_2dr_1+\cdots)A(s)$. If $\|K\|\le M$, the $n$th term has norm at most $M^n/n!$. Derivatives in the compact parameter $s$ are bounded by the same factorial denominator times a polynomial in $n$ and bounds for finitely many derivatives of $K$; the series and all these derivatives converge uniformly. Differentiation in $r$ follows from its integral equation, giving a smooth periodic family. Uniqueness follows by iterating the integral inequality for the difference of two solutions: its supremum is bounded by $M^n/n!$ times that supremum for every $n$, hence is zero. The derivative of $F^*F$ is zero, so $F$ is unitary. The determinant derivative is $\det F\operatorname{tr}(F^{-1}KF)=0$, hence $\det F=1$. The first column and $v(s,r)$ satisfy the same ODE with the same initial value, so they agree. At $r=1$ the loop therefore has the block form $\operatorname{diag}(1,A_1(s))$ with $A_1(s)\in SU(m-1)$.

**Finish the contraction and fill the disk.** Repeat the first-column contraction and matrix-ODE lift on the smaller special unitary block. Finite induction on $m$, ending with $SU(1)=\{1\}$, contracts the original special unitary loop to the identity. Combine this with step 2.1. Smoothly reparametrize each homotopy to be stationary near its two time endpoints before concatenation; the result is a smooth homotopy $H(s,r)$ from $G$ at $r=0$ to the constant identity at $r=1$. In polar coordinates put $\widehat G(\rho e^{2\pi i s})=H(s,\sigma(\rho))$, where $\sigma=0$ near $\rho=1$ and $\sigma=1$ near $\rho=0$. It is smooth at the center because it is constant there, and it is independent of radius near the boundary. It stays invertible throughout the homotopy. Together with step 1.1 this proves the equivalence for a prescribed boundary loop.

**Preserve prescribed collar data.** Let $C(\rho,s)$ be the given smooth invertible matrix map for $c<\rho\le1$. Choose $c<c_1<c_2<1$ and a smooth radial function $f$ on $[c_1,1]$ equal to the identity near $1$ and to $c_2$ near $c_1$, with values in $(c,1]$. Then $C(f(\rho),s)$ retains the original map on a smaller outer collar and is independent of radius on an inner collar. Its inner loop has the same determinant winding as the original boundary loop by step 1.1. If that winding is zero, step 5.1 fills the inner loop with the same radius-independent collar; rescale its disk and paste along the constant collar. The maps and all derivatives agree there. Necessity still follows from step 1.1. This proves the stronger relative statement, with only finite-dimensional formulas, ordinary one-variable integrals and finite induction.

citations.quote:
Let $m\ge1$ and let $G:\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\to\operatorname{GL}_m(\mathbb C)$ be smooth. Its determinant winding is the integer
$$w(G)=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_0^1\frac{(\det G)'(s)}{\det G(s)}\,ds.$$
There is a smooth map $\widehat G:\overline{\mathbb D}\to\operatorname{GL}_m(\mathbb C)$ restricting to $G$ on the positively oriented boundary if and only if $w(G)=0$. When it exists the extension can be chosen independent of radius on a boundary collar. More generally a prescribed smooth invertible matrix map on a collar of the disk boundary extends smoothly to the disk, agreeing on a smaller boundary collar, exactly when its boundary determinant winding is zero. The construction is finite dimensional and choice-free.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\vartheta:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be a smooth real function constant at values $\vartheta_-$ and $\vartheta_+$ on the two ends, with $\vartheta_\pm\notin\pi\mathbb Z$. On $S=\mathbb R_s\times[0,1]_t$, let $X_\vartheta$ be the $H^1$ completion of smooth complex-valued maps compactly supported in $s$, with $u(s,0)\in\mathbb R$ and $u(s,1)\in e^{i\vartheta(s)}\mathbb R$. Let $A(s,t):\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$ be an essentially bounded measurable real linear map tending to zero uniformly in essential supremum on both ends. Then
$$\mathcal D=\partial_s+i\partial_t+A:X_\vartheta\longrightarrow L^2(S;\mathbb C)$$
is bounded Fredholm over $\mathbb R$, before taking any quotient by translation, and
$$\operatorname{ind}_{\mathbb R}\mathcal D=\left\lfloor\frac{\vartheta_-}\pi\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor\frac{\vartheta_+}\pi\right\rfloor.$$
The same index holds on the spaces weighted by $e^{\delta|s|}$ when $0\le\delta<\min_{\pm}\operatorname{dist}(\vartheta_\pm,\pi\mathbb Z)$. In particular, if the upper line is the same at both ends and $\vartheta_+-\vartheta_-=k\pi$, its fixed-end strip index is $-k$. This sign uses the orientation $ds\wedge dt$ and the operator $\partial_s+i\partial_t$: the oriented upper boundary runs from $s=+\infty$ to $s=-\infty$.

Componentwise the same result holds for finitely many given angle functions $\vartheta_j(s)$, the product upper boundary $\prod_j e^{i\vartheta_j(s)}\mathbb R$, and any bounded real linear matrix $A(s,t)$ tending to zero: the real index is the sum of their displayed floor differences. This is an explicit globally framed boundary-line result; it does not supply a global frame for a general geometric strip or identify its index with a Heegaard-domain expression.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,g)$ be compact, let $L_0,L_1\subset X$ be compact smooth half-dimensional submanifolds with finite intersection, and let $J(s,t,x)$ be smooth almost complex structures on $[0,\infty)\times[0,1]\times X$ with uniform $C^2$ bounds in source and target. Assume $J(s,j,x)=J_{b,j}(x)$ for $x\in L_j$, independent of $s$, and that $L_j$ is totally real for $J_{b,j}$. A smooth solution
$$u_s+J(s,t,u)u_t=0,\qquad u(s,j)\in L_j,$$
with finite Dirichlet energy has a unique point $x_+\in L_0\cap L_1$ such that
$$\sup_{0\le t\le1}d_g(u(s,t),x_+)\longrightarrow0,\qquad \sup_{0\le t\le1}|du(s,t)|_g\longrightarrow0$$
as $s\to\infty$. In particular no such strip exists if $L_0\cap L_1$ is empty. Compact transverse half-dimensional $L_0,L_1$ satisfy the finite-intersection premise. The analogous conclusion holds at a negative strip end. No exponential rate or index theorem is asserted.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Sigma$ be a closed oriented smooth surface with positive area form $\eta$ and an orientation-compatible complex structure $j$. Use its smooth complex symmetric product $X=\operatorname{Sym}^m\Sigma$, $m\ge1$, and the descended product symplectic form $\omega$ off the diagonal. Let $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_m$ be disjoint embedded circles, and likewise $\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_m$, with every alpha-beta intersection transverse. Let $T_\alpha,T_\beta\subset X$ be their product tori. Fix finitely many points $p$ of $\Sigma$ away from all these circles and the associated divisors $E_p=\{p\}+\operatorname{Sym}^{m-1}\Sigma$.

The intersection $K=T_\alpha\cap T_\beta$ is finite and disjoint from the diagonal and all $E_p$. There exist pairwise disjoint neighborhoods $U_x$ of its points, with closures disjoint from those protected sets, and smooth coordinate charts $q_x$ centered at $x$ taking $T_\alpha,T_\beta$ to $\mathbb R^m,i\mathbb R^m$. There is a smooth almost complex structure $J_*$ on $X$ equal to $\operatorname{Sym}^m(j)$ near the diagonal and all $E_p$, taming $\omega$ elsewhere, and exactly $i$ in each $q_x$ chart near $x$.

More generally any smooth family $J_t$ with the first two properties can be modified inside the $U_x$, retaining its values outside them and near all protected sets, to have those exact product-integrable values on smaller neighborhoods for every $t$. The constant path $J_*$ therefore provides a genuine admissible geometric choice with the local hypotheses needed for product-integrable end asymptotics. No regularity or moduli count is asserted for that path.

derivations.claim: **A complex frame on a compact core, constructed rather than assumed.** Choose $R$ large enough that the stated end frames and exact operator expressions hold on neighborhoods of the vertical edges of the rectangle $Q=[-R,R]\times[0,1]$. The complex bundle on this rectangle has a finite complex-chart cover: locally choose $m$ real vectors whose images with their $J$ multiples form a basis at a point; their linear independence persists nearby, giving a complex chart. Compactness gives finitely many such charts $g_a:E\to\mathbb C^m$ and smooth nonnegative bumps $\beta_a$ supported in them with $\sum_a\beta_a^2>0$. These bumps can be made from finitely many smaller coordinate rectangles using the ordinary explicit smooth bump on a Euclidean ball. The map $I_x(v)=(\beta_a(x)g_a(v))_a$ embeds each fiber complex linearly in one fixed $\mathbb C^N$; zero extension is smooth because each bump has support inside its chart. Orthogonal projection $Q_x$ onto its image is smooth: in a local complex frame with image-column matrix $V_x$, it is $V_x(V_x^*V_x)^{-1}V_x^*$. Fix a basis in the image at one point $x_0$ of the rectangle and transport it to $x$ along $x_r=x_0+r(x-x_0)$ by the matrix equation $Z_r=[(Q_{x_r})_r,Q_{x_r}]Z$. The coefficient is skew-Hermitian. The identity $Q Q_r Q=0$, obtained by differentiating $Q^2=Q$, shows that a transported vector initially in the image stays in the image. Its norm and all inner products are preserved. The iterated-integral series has term bounds $M^n/n!$ on the compact parameter set; differentiating in $x$ adds only polynomial factors in $n$ and finite derivative bounds, so it gives a smooth family and a unique solution. Pulling the transported basis back by $I_x$ yields a smooth complex frame $\Psi$ on the whole rectangle. Thus contractibility of the base has not been substituted for a relative boundary framing argument.

**Real frames and their endpoint orientation signs.** In $\Psi$ coordinates each $F_j$ is a smooth real rank-$m$ subbundle of $\mathbb R^{2m}$ along an interval. Its real orthogonal projection $Q_j(s)$ is smooth by the same finite matrix formula. The real equation $h'_j=[Q'_j,Q_j]h_j$, starting with any ordered basis in its initial fiber, transports a smooth real basis along the whole edge, by the same series and projection identities as in step 1.1. Start the lower basis at $\tau_-\mathbb R^m$ and the upper basis at $\tau_- i\mathbb R^m$. On the positive end compare the transported lower basis with $\tau_+$ and the transported upper basis with $\tau_+ i$. Let their real determinant signs be $\sigma_0,\sigma_1\in\{1,-1\}$. Set $S_+=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_0,1,\ldots,1)$ and choose the unique $p\in\{0,1\}$ with $\sigma_0(-1)^p=\sigma_1$. The desired lower terminal basis $\tau_+S_+$ and upper terminal basis $\tau_+S_+\operatorname{diag}(i(-1)^p,i,\ldots,i)$ then have the same orientations as the respective transported bases. We may correct the transported bases by smooth real matrices to obtain frames $f_0(s),f_1(s)$ equal to those specified bases on entire end collars, and to the initial specified bases on the negative collar. Here is the needed path construction: real matrices of positive determinant can be joined to the identity using row-addition paths $I+t cE_{ab}$ to diagonalize, positive diagonal rescalings, and planar rotations removing pairs of negative diagonal entries. A zero pivot can first be made nonzero by adding a row with a nonzero entry, so no row permutation of negative determinant is required. There are finitely many steps. On each end collar the correction matrix has positive determinant; flatten its source coordinate on an inner collar, join its resulting constant value to the identity by this finite path, and retain its original values on a smaller outer collar. This matches all derivatives where pieces are pasted.

**The boundary frame loop and its actual obstruction.** Choose a smooth cutoff $\chi(s)$ equal to zero on the negative collar and one on the positive collar. First put $\vartheta_0(s)=\pi/2+p\pi\chi(s)$. Prescribe a complex frame along the rectangle boundary as follows: on the bottom it is $f_0(s)$; on the top it is $f_1(s)\operatorname{diag}(e^{-i\vartheta_0(s)},-i,\ldots,-i)$; on the left it is $\tau_-$; on the right it is $\tau_+S_+$. The columns of $f_j$ are complex linearly independent, since $F_j\cap JF_j=0$: a complex dependence has real and imaginary parts in $F_j$ whose $J$ images coincide, forcing both to vanish. Thus these are invertible complex frames. Their values agree on the corner collars by step 2.1. Express them in the global core frame $\Psi$ to obtain an invertible matrix loop $G$, oriented by $ds\wedge dt$ on the rectangle. Round the four corners inside their end-frame neighborhoods and use the already specified end frame along each rounded arc. This gives a smooth matrix loop on the rounded core; the old edge path and rounded arc are homotopic within that end neighborhood, so their determinant windings agree. Let $k=w(G)\in\mathbb Z$. The lower orientation correction alone has not forced this integer to vanish.

**Absorb the winding and extend the frame relative to the ends.** Replace the top angle by $\vartheta(s)=\vartheta_0(s)-2\pi k\chi(s)$. The new top frame differs from the old one by $\operatorname{diag}(e^{2\pi i k\chi(s)},1,\ldots,1)$. The oriented top edge is traversed from $s=R$ to $s=-R$, so this changes determinant winding by $-k$. The new boundary loop therefore has winding zero; its negative and positive angle limits are $\pi/2$ and $\pi/2+\ell\pi$, where $\ell=p-2k$. It retains exactly the prescribed vertical frames because the added end phases are integer multiples of $2\pi$. Extend the boundary matrix data to a thin collar in $Q$, keeping them equal to $\Psi^{-1}\tau_-$ and $\Psi^{-1}\tau_+S_+$ on smaller vertical collars. Such collar data can be built locally by extending each edge matrix in its normal direction; near a corner the vertical data are already smooth invertible matrices on a full corner neighborhood and agree with the horizontal edge data. Shrink the remaining collars so all overlapping values lie in a small convex matrix ball contained in $\operatorname{GL}_m(\mathbb C)$, and patch with finitely many scalar bumps, retaining the exact edge and vertical values. The relative-collar part of [F1] now fills this zero-winding matrix map on the rounded core disk. Multiplying the filling by $\Psi$ and retaining the given end frames on the removed corner neighborhoods gives $\Phi$ on the whole core rectangle. It equals the specified vertical frames on collars, so extends to all $S$ by $\tau_-$ and $\tau_+S_+$ on the ends. Its two horizontal boundary frames give exactly the two subbundle identities in the Statement.

**Identify the actual operator and Sobolev domains.** A finite collection of smooth bundle charts on the compact core, with compactly supported scalar cutoffs and the two given end frames, defines an $H^1$ norm on compactly supported smooth sections. Any two such choices give equivalent norms: chart transition matrices and their first derivatives are bounded on the finitely many compact overlaps, and outside the core both use the given end frames. The same argument applies to the $L^2$ target norm. Multiplication by $\Phi$ and $\Phi^{-1}$ is bounded for these norms, because their matrices and first derivatives are bounded on the compact core and they are the constant comparisons $I,S_+$ on the ends. They send the actual compactly supported smooth boundary sections bijectively to the scalar/product-line sections prescribed by $\vartheta$, hence identify their completions. The symbol identity and $\Phi i=J\Phi$ show that $\Phi^{-1}P\Phi$ has principal part $\partial_s+i\partial_t$. To see this directly, write a section as a sum of the $2m$ real coordinate functions times $\Phi e_a$ and $J\Phi e_a$ and apply the stated real Leibniz identity to each summand. The remaining terms define a smooth real linear multiplication matrix $B$. On the ends $\Phi$ is the given end frame times the constant $I$ or $S_+$, and the operator there is exactly $D$; thus $B=0$ there. It is therefore compactly supported and bounded. This establishes the normal form for the actual operator and its domain, rather than assuming them from its principal symbol alone.

**Fredholm index and weights.** Apply [F2] to the operator of step 5.1. The first upper angle has end values $\pi/2$ and $\pi/2+\ell\pi$; every other angle is constantly $\pi/2$. The floor differences are consequently $0-\ell=-\ell$ for the first component and zero for the rest. Thus $P$ is Fredholm with real index $-\ell$. All limiting product-angle spectra have gap $\pi/2$, so [F2] also applies with every $0\le\delta<\pi/2$. The frame comparison commutes with the scalar weight and remains bounded on weighted completions by the same compact-core estimates. Source and target isomorphisms preserve kernel, range and cokernel, proving the weighted claim for $P$. Different choices of frames, real basis signs or filling which meet the same hypotheses still compute this fixed Fredholm operator's index, so they give the same integer $\ell$. Nothing has been subtracted for source translation.

**Apply this to the actual geometric linearization.** Let $u$ be the smooth finite-energy strip in the last clause. By [F3], its two far ends lie in the specified generator charts. There the nonlinear equation is exactly $v_s+i v_t=0$ in target coordinates, so its coordinate linearization is exactly $D=\partial_s+i\partial_t$, with boundary variations in $\mathbb R^m,i\mathbb R^m$. On the whole strip put $E=u^*TX$, $J(s,t)=J_t(u(s,t))$ and $F_j=u(\cdot,j)^*TL_j$. These are smooth bundles with $F_j\cap JF_j=0$ by the given totally real hypothesis. The coordinate formula for the actual real linearization at a solution is $P\xi=\xi_s+J_t(u)\xi_t+(dJ_t)_u[\xi]u_t$. It has exactly the stated symbol. These local formulas transform as a bundle operator: differentiating a change of target coordinates introduces its derivative on the Cauchy–Riemann section, whose value at this solution is zero, so no extra principal or residual term occurs. Equivalently the covariant and coordinate formulas agree after the corresponding source and target bundle identification. Thus all hypotheses of the frame, normal-form and index arguments above hold, proving the claimed actual real $H^1$ Fredholm theorem. For product Heegaard tori their Lagrangian tangent spaces are totally real for a tame $J$: a nonzero $v$ with $v,Jv$ both tangent would give $\omega(v,Jv)=0$, contradicting tameness. The geometric product charts and the simultaneous all-$t$ exact values of $J_t$ are supplied by [F4]. This completes the asserted application, while the equality with domain Euler measure and corner multiplicities still requires separate corner, excision and domain-comparison proofs.
